Recent? I have no idea. I just took my knowledge and experience with cars, jets, and electronics, looked at Frozencpu.com, TomsHardware, and DangerDen.com (and newegg/tigerdirect/amazon/etc). I planned ahead on a notebook for a few weeks getting the design correct, then ordered all the parts when I got back home from deployment. Took about 2 weeks to build and overclock correctly.

I do recommend a non-conductive fluid be used, especially if it's your first time. Placing a few paper towels under any new fittings helps to narrow down any leaks and keeps that wet stuff off your gear. As far as keeping it silent:

 

Fans: Bigger, slower, and fewer is generally better. Look at reviews to determine actual airflow and decibel output as most manufacturers will lie. More airflow = good, more decibels = bad.

Water pump: Almost anything that can move water will work but something specifically designed to run quietly within a PC case will work better than other options (like fish tank or well pumps). Get some foam or rubber to put between the pump and where you mount it to help keep it quiet.

Tubing: Thicker tube walls matter more than throughput if you are looking for silent and don't want those things kinking up. The bigger the difference between ID (Inner Diameter) and OD (Outer Diameter) the thicker the tube wall is.

Radiator: Biggest you can fit, match the fans up for size, and get either rubber or foam to slap between the two to keep down the rattling. Aim it to blow out of the case so you don't draw in extra heat from the radiator.

Cooling blocks: Use whatever fits. Some perform a bit better than others, but if it doesn't fit right it just won't work. Usually people get one for the CPU and the video card. Occasionally you see some for the RAM and the north/south bridge. If you are handy you can build your own adapters but that's a pain in the ass (I should know).

Connectors: Try to keep them all the same size, it helps when you are swapping stuff around.

 

Other stuff: plumber's tape, it really does help! Sound dampening material doesn't need to be expensive to work effectively, but it does take time and effort to install properly. Use a proper razor-cutter to trim it to size. Take the time to think about where you air is coming from and where it is going before you buy a single thing. This of course means you have an idea of what case you are trying to fit all this crap into. Don't forget about the fan in the PSU, it could be silent or it could sound like a jet about to take off. If the holes don't line up and you end up having to drill into your case remove everything before you grab the drill. Trust me, you don't want to be JB-welding your brand-new radiator because it was "only a small hole". Put the entire water-cooling loop together, put your fluid in, and run the pump without the electronics anywhere near it for about a day. Place towels underneath, it will leak from somewhere.

Good luck!

Keep in mind the idea behind using a water-cooling setup to silence a PC. You are taking the heat away (via water, tubing, and pump) from something with a small surface area (the top of your CPU) to something with a much larger surface area (the radiator). This allows you to remove the smaller, faster, and (usually) louder fan from the CPU and replace it with a larger, slower, and quieter fan on the radiator. You could use the system to simply replace the air cooling and get a giant howling tornado of a fan and overclock the bajeesus out of it (lots of people go that route), but that sort of defeats the purpose of silencing the machine.

Oh, and a reservoir is useful to help keep evaporation, eddy currents, and air bubbles from messing up your system.

Edit: and something I forgot. Certain fan controllers allow you to under-volt and over-volt the fans so you can adjust the noise level to your liking or needs.
